1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Example 16 17 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 18 19 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 20 21 You can find the resources used in this example here: 22 23 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 24 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 25 26 Before starting, enable view transitions in your Next.js config: 27 28 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 29 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 30 31 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 32 experimental: { 33 viewTransition: true, 34 }, 35 } 36 37 export default nextConfig 38 ``` 39 40 > [!NOTE] 41 > The View Transitions API is supported in all major browsers, though some animations may behave differently in Safari. 301	
302	```css filename="app/globals.css"
303	::view-transition-group(site-header) {
304	  animation: none;
305	  z-index: 100;
306	}
307	::view-transition-old(site-header) {
308	  display: none;
309	}
310	::view-transition-new(site-header) {
311	  animation: none;
312	}
313	```
314	
315	The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content.
316	
317	If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions.
318	
319	Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props.
320	
321	#### Respecting reduced motion
322	
323	Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position.
324	
325	The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations:
326	
327	```css filename="app/globals.css"
328	@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
329	  ::view-transition-old(*),
330	  ::view-transition-new(*),
331	  ::view-transition-group(*) {
332	    animation-duration: 0s !important;
333	    animation-delay: 0s !important;
334	  }
335	}
336	```
337	
338	Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this.
339	
340	### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route
341	
342	The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container.
343	
344	A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap).
345	
346	Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content:
347	
348	```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx"
349	import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react'
350	
351	export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) {
352	  const { slug } = await params
353	
354	  return (
355	    <Suspense fallback={<CollectionGridSkeleton />}>
356	      <ViewTransition
357	        key={slug}
358	        name="collection-content"
359	        share="auto"
360	        enter="auto"
361	        default="none"
362	      >
363	        <CollectionGrid slug={slug} />
364	      </ViewTransition>
365	    </Suspense>
366	  )
367	}
368	```
369	
370	The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The `key={slug}` change is what triggers the transition.
371	
372	If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states.
373	
374	## Next steps
375	
376	You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location.
377	
378	Each pattern answers a different question for the user:
379	
380	| Pattern                | What it communicates            |
381	| ---------------------- | ------------------------------- |
382	| Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper"      |
383	| Suspense reveal        | "Data loaded"                   |
384	| Directional slide      | "Going forward / coming back"   |
385	| Same-route crossfade   | "Same place, different content" |
386	
387	For API details and more patterns:
388	
389	- [View transition configuration](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/viewTransition)
390	- [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes)
391	- [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router) — also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()`
392	- [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition)
393	- [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file

Everything builds and looks correct. Here's a summary of what was added:

**Config** (`next.config.ts`): Enabled `experimental.viewTransition`

**Shared element morph** — Both `ProductGrid.tsx` and the detail page wrap product images in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph">`. The matching `name` causes the browser to animate the thumbnail morphing into the hero (and back) during navigation. The morph uses a 400ms cubic-bezier easing.

**Directional page slides** — Both pages wrap their content in `<ViewTransition name="page-content">` with `enter`/`exit` maps keyed by transition type. Grid links use `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`, the back link uses `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}`. CSS slides content left (60px) for forward nav and right for back nav, with staggered fade timing (150ms exit, 210ms enter).

**Suspense reveal** — The skeleton fallback has `exit="slide-down"`, the content wrapper has `enter="slide-up"`. When async data resolves, the skeleton slides down/fades out, then real content slides up/fades in with a slight delay.

**Reduced motion** — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` sets all view transition animation durations and delays to `0s`, making swaps instant. Skeleton pulse animations are also disabled.
